1282.title: The Healer's Blessed Hands
1282.hook: a Vedic healer blesses their own two hands, and Hindus still greet the divine in their palms each morning
1282.carry: the sacred is in your hands: see them first
1282.tomorrow: what do Hindu families chant for someone who's sick?
1282.howItsDone: Many Hindus begin the day with kara darshan, looking into their palms and naming Lakshmi, Saraswati and Govinda; elders bless with a hand on the head; Vedic verses for the sick are kept in recitation learned from a teacher.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn bowed to a fever: namah, bow even to the power you fear, then ask it to go. Today, a hymn that ends at the healer's own hands.
screen: `NAMAH: BOW, THEN ASK IT TO PASS.`

segments.voice: A hand on a forehead. It's the check that comes before any thermometer. Someone leans over a sick child, lays a palm there, and the hand asks a question: hot, or not? But something else happens too. The child's shoulders drop a little. Somebody is here. The hand is part of the answer before anyone knows what the answer is. One healing hymn in the Atharva Veda ends right at that spot: not with an herb, not with a potion, but with the healer looking down at their own two hands and speaking to them.
screen: `A HAND ON A FOREHEAD.` → `SOMEBODY IS HERE.` → `A HYMN SPEAKS TO THE HANDS.`

segments.voice: The Atharva Veda keeps hymns for the bedside, and one of them, in its fourth book, opens with a plea: you gods, raise up again the one who has fallen. Then the healer turns, not to the patient and not to a god, but to their own hands. In paraphrase: this hand of mine is blessed. This other hand is more blessed still. This one holds every remedy, vishvabheshaja, all-healing. This one's touch is kind. And then: with these two hands of ten branches, and with the tongue that goes before speech, with these two healing hands, we touch you. Hands and voice together, and the hands themselves called holy. That idea didn't stay in the Veda. Many Hindus begin every day with a short Sanskrit prayer called kara darshan, seeing the hands. Before the phone, before the floor, you look into your open palms and say: at the fingertips lives Lakshmi, Goddess of plenty; in the middle, Saraswati, Goddess of learning; at the base, Govinda, Krishna. Families say it a little differently, but the teaching is the same: the hands that will cook, write, work and care today are a home for the divine. An elder's blessing, too, comes as a hand on the head. So the hands you bring to a sickbed, or to a sink full of dishes, aren't just tools. In this tradition, they're where the day's work becomes worship.
screen: `RAISE UP THE ONE WHO FELL.` · `THIS HAND BLESSED, THIS ONE MORE BLESSED.` · `KARA DARSHAN: SEEING THE HANDS.` · `THE DAY'S WORK BECOMES WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: Open your hands in front of you, palms up, the way many Hindus do on waking. Look at the fingertips, then the middle of the palms, then the base, near the wrist. If you pray, say the names as you go, Lakshmi, Saraswati, Govinda, and offer what these hands will do today. If you don't, simply look, and think of one person your hands will care for before the day is out.

1283.title: Chanting for the Sick
1283.hook: an old hymn sends a cough flying, and families still chant a Rig Veda verse at the bedside
1283.carry: hindus chant for the sick, alongside the medicine
1283.tomorrow: why do so many Hindu homes water one plant every morning?
1283.howItsDone: Vedic hymns for the sick are kept in recitation from teacher to student; many Hindu families chant the Mahamrityunjaya mantra, often 108 times on a mala, for someone who is ill, alongside medical care.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a healer spoke to a pair of hands, vishvabheshaja, all-healing: the sacred is in your hands, see them first.
screen: `THE SACRED IS IN YOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: Some ailments get a lecture. Some get a bargain. In one short Atharva Veda hymn, a cough gets something stranger: directions. Three verses, and in each one the speaker points the cough toward the horizon and tells it to go. Not to die, just to leave, fast and far. Anyone propped up on pillows at night, tired of the rattle in their chest, knows the wish. Here it's poetry, all speed and distance.
screen: `A LECTURE, A BARGAIN, OR DIRECTIONS?` → `GO. FAST, AND FAR.`

segments.voice: Here is the hymn, in paraphrase. As the mind, with its wishes, flies swiftly far away, so, cough, fly off along the mind's own course. As a sharpened arrow flies swiftly far, so, cough, fly off across the wide earth. As the rays of the sun fly swiftly far, so, cough, fly off along the surge of the sea. The cough is kasa, and the hymn speaks straight to it, as if words could reach it. That's the Vedic faith in speech: a mantra said with care is an act, not just a sound. And it's why Hindu families still chant for the sick. The verse many turn to comes from the Rig Veda: the Mahamrityunjaya, the great death-conquering mantra. Families tie it to the story of Markandeya, a boy fated to die at sixteen. When Yama, lord of death, threw his noose, the boy held tight to a Shiva linga, and Shiva burst out of it and drove death back. Om tryambakam yajamahe. In paraphrase: we worship the three-eyed one, Shiva, fragrant, who makes life grow. As a ripe cucumber slips from its vine, may I be freed from death, not from the deathless. Families chant it a hundred and eight times on a mala, play it softly by a hospital bed, or gather on a call to say it together. Many teachers read what it asks this way: not never to die, to be let go gently, like ripe fruit, toward what doesn't die. And to be plain: this is prayer, not treatment. Hindus chant beside the doctor's care, never instead of it, and a cough that hangs on belongs with a doctor.
screen: `AS THE MIND FLIES, FLY OFF.` · `A MANTRA IS AN ACT, NOT JUST A SOUND.` · `OM TRYAMBAKAM YAJAMAHE.` · `PRAYER BESIDE THE MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who is unwell. If you pray, say the mantra's opening slowly, om tryambakam yajamahe, or simply their name, three times, the way many Hindus pray for the sick. If you don't, hold that person in mind for three slow breaths and wish them well. Then pick one plain thing to do for them today: a text, a meal, a call.

1284.title: Plants Called Mothers
1284.hook: the Vedas call the plants mothers, which is why so many Hindu homes water a tulsi every morning
1284.carry: the plants are mothers: why hindus water the tulsi
1284.tomorrow: why do Hindus sip water from the palm before worship?
1284.howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a tulsi plant, honored as a goddess and dear to Vishnu, watering it each morning and lighting a lamp beside it at dusk; the Vedic hymns to the plants are kept in recitation, and Ayurvedic tradition later developed its own learning about plants.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn sent a cough flying: Hindus chant for the sick, alongside the medicine.
screen: `PRAYER BESIDE THE MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Brown, white, red, dappled, dark. That's not a paint chart. It's how one Atharva Veda hymn begins its roll call of the plants. Before it asks them for anything, it looks at them and sorts them by color, the way a kid sorts crayons or a cook lines up vegetables on a cutting board. An empty lot in summer holds the same crowd: weeds, wildflowers and grasses, many without a name to a passerby. The hymn calls them up one color at a time, and then calls them all.
screen: `BROWN, WHITE, RED, DAPPLED, DARK.` → `NOT A PAINT CHART.` → `A ROLL CALL OF PLANTS.`

segments.voice: The Atharva Veda's long hymn to the plants opens, in paraphrase: the brown ones, the white, the red, the dappled, the dark and the black, all the plants, we call on. It asks them to protect the one who is sick. The Rig Veda has a hymn to the plants too, the oshadhi, plants that heal, and it tells a small scene. The plants gather and talk together with Soma, their king, and make a promise: whoever the priest tends for healing, O king, we carry across to safety. And it speaks to them with a startling word: plants, mothers, I speak to you as goddesses. Mothers. Not ingredients. That's a Hindu teaching you can see from the street. In many Hindu homes, in a courtyard in India or a pot on a New Jersey porch, stands a tulsi, holy basil, honored as a goddess and dear to Vishnu. Every morning someone waters it, often with a prayer, and many light a small lamp beside it at dusk. The teaching under it: the divine isn't kept in temples only; the green world is alive with it, and you treat it the way you'd treat a mother. One honest note: these hymns aren't prescriptions, and nothing here says what to take for an illness. They teach how to look. A plant in a pot can be decoration, or it can be family.
screen: `ALL THE PLANTS, CALLED BY COLOR.` · `PLANTS, MOTHERS, GODDESSES.` · `TULSI: WATERED EVERY MORNING.` · `THE GREEN WORLD IS ALIVE WITH GOD.`

segments.voice: Find something green: a houseplant, a tree outside the window, herbs on the counter. If there's water near, give it a little, the way many Hindus water the tulsi each morning. If you pray, thank it the way you'd thank a mother. If you don't, simply name its color as plainly as the hymn does, and think of what it took to grow.

1285.title: Medicine in the Waters
1285.hook: the Vedas find medicine in the waters, so Hindu worship begins with water: sipped, sprinkled, offered
1285.carry: water purifies: sip it, sprinkle it, offer it
1285.howItsDone: Many Hindus begin worship with achamana, three sips of water from the palm; the Vedic verses to the waters (apo hi shtha) are said while sprinkling water in the daily sandhya; water is offered to the sun, and Ganga water is kept at home for the sick and the dying.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-TWO-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the plants are mothers: spoken to as goddesses, and a tulsi watered every morning.
screen: `THE PLANTS ARE MOTHERS.`

segments.voice: A glass of water on a nightstand. It's the first thing reached for in the morning and the last thing set down at night. Nobody calls it medicine. It just sits there, sweating a ring onto the wood. The Atharva Veda doesn't overlook it. In its first book, among the healing hymns, are verses spoken to the waters. Today is also the last day on the Vedas themselves, so after the waters, a look back.
screen: `A GLASS OF WATER ON A NIGHTSTAND.` → `NOBODY CALLS IT MEDICINE.` → `THE VEDA DOES.`

segments.voice: One verse, in paraphrase: you waters are the ones who bring us joy; help us to strength, so that we may see great delight. Another: within the waters is the deathless drink, within the waters is medicine. Another asks the divine waters to be kind to us, for our help and for our drinking. The word for medicine is bheshaja, the word inside the healer's all-healing hand. In these hymns the waters heal, delight, and are goddesses. That's why water stands at the start of so much Hindu worship. Before a puja, many sip a little water from the right palm three times, often with a name of Vishnu each time: achamana, cleansing from the inside. In the daily prayer called sandhya, these very verses, apo hi shtha, you waters are, are said while water is sprinkled over the head. Water is poured out to the rising sun, and many homes keep a small sealed pot of water from the Ganga, a few drops given to the sick or the dying. The teaching: water purifies, body and mind, and it's holy enough to begin anything sacred. And today closes the Vedas themselves: from the creation hymn and the cosmic person, through the Gayatri, Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna and the sung Sama Veda, down to a glass of water by a sickbed. Next, Ayurveda.
screen: `IN THE WATERS, MEDICINE.` · `ACHAMANA: THREE SIPS BEFORE WORSHIP.` · `APO HI SHTHA: WATER SPRINKLED.` · `THE VEDAS, FROM CREATION TO A SICKBED.`

segments.voice: If there's water near you, pour a little into your right palm. If you pray, sip it three times, the way many Hindus do before worship, with a name of God each time. If you don't, take one slow sip and follow it, cool on the lips, across the tongue, down the throat, and let it mark a fresh start.

1286.title: Dhanvantari and the Three Doshas
1286.word: the three doshas as a way of noticing

segments.voice: Two days before Diwali, many Hindu families buy something new for the house, a steel pot, a spoon, sometimes a little gold, and set a lamp by the door. The day is Dhanteras. Most people think of it as a day for wealth. But it's also kept as the birthday of a god who walked out of the ocean holding a pot, and in that pot was the cure for death itself. He's honored as the god of a whole tradition of medicine, and that's where this path turns now: Ayurveda, held here as a lens for noticing, never as a diagnosis.

segments.voice: It's one of the great scenes in Hindu story. The gods and the asuras churn the ocean of milk for amrita, the drink of immortality. Wonder after wonder rises out of the foam, and then a shining figure steps up carrying a pot: Dhanvantari, holding the amrita itself. The Bhagavata Purana counts him among the forms of Vishnu, and Hindus honor him as the god of Ayurveda, a name that means the knowledge, veda, of life, ayus. The Sushruta Samhita calls Ayurveda a branch of the Atharva Veda: the healing hymns of last week, grown up. On Dhanteras many families pray to Dhanvantari for health, beside Lakshmi for plenty. So here's the teaching: in this tradition, caring for a body is holy work. Healing rose out of the same ocean as the gods' nectar. Ayurveda's first vocabulary is three words. The Ashtanga Hridaya, in paraphrase: wind, bile and phlegm; in brief, these are the three doshas, vata, pitta and kapha. Vata moves: breath, a darting thought. Pitta heats and changes: digestion, a flash of temper. Kapha holds: weight, steadiness. All three are forces in every body, at once. Ayurveda has its own trained practitioners. On this path the doshas are held one way only, as a way of noticing, never a diagnosis; questions about your health belong with a doctor.
screen: `DHANVANTARI RISES WITH THE AMRITA.` · `AYURVEDA: THE KNOWLEDGE OF LIFE.` · `VATA MOVES. PITTA HEATS. KAPHA HOLDS.` · `A WAY OF NOTICING, NOT A DIAGNOSIS.`

segments.voice: Find something moving: the breath, going in and out on its own. Then something warm, your palms or the air in your mouth, and something steady, the weight of your body on the seat. Let all three be there at once, without deciding anything about them. If you pray, ask for health the way families do on Dhanteras, for yourself and for someone you love.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Vata, pitta, kapha: what moves, what heats, what holds.

segments.voice: Puja day in a lot of Hindu homes comes with a quiet kitchen rule: no onion, no garlic, not today. Ask why and you might get a shrug, a story, or just: that's how Grandma does it. The reason goes back to one Sanskrit word. Ayurveda uses it to describe the doshas. And Krishna uses it on a battlefield, of all places, to talk about what's for lunch.
screen: `NO ONION, NO GARLIC, NOT TODAY.` → `ONE SANSKRIT WORD.` → `KRISHNA ON LUNCH.`

segments.voice: The Ashtanga Hridaya describes each dosha by its qualities. In paraphrase: vata is dry, light, cold, rough, subtle and moving. Pitta is a little oily, sharp, hot, light and flowing. Kapha is oily, cold, heavy, slow, smooth and steady. The word for a quality is guna. And that word leads straight into a scene Hindus know well. In the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna about people's faith, and Krishna answers that faith, and nearly everything else, comes in three gunas: sattva, clear and bright; rajas, restless and driven; tamas, heavy and dull. Even food. In paraphrase: foods dear to the sattvic increase life, strength, health and joy; they're juicy, smooth, nourishing and pleasant. Rajasic foods are too bitter, sour, salty, hot and burning, and bring pain and grief. Tamasic food is stale, tasteless, gone off, left over. This is the teaching behind a lot of Hindu kitchens. Many families keep puja and temple food sattvic, and some leave out onion and garlic altogether; teachers commonly explain them as rajasic or tamasic, stirring up or dulling the mind. Not every Hindu home does this, and nobody's ranked by their plate. But the idea runs deep: what you eat doesn't stop at the body. It colors the mind you bring to prayer. On this path the doshas stay a way of noticing, never a diagnosis; the gunas ask a different question: is this meal for a clear mind?
screen: `THE DOSHAS BY THEIR GUNAS.` · `SATTVA, RAJAS, TAMAS: EVEN FOOD.` · `WHY NO ONION OR GARLIC.` · `FOOD FOR A CLEAR MIND.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, pause over the plate. Notice its qualities the way the texts do: warm or cool, heavy or light, fresh or not. If you pray, offer it first, as many Hindus do, and ask that it make your mind clear. If you don't, eat the first three bites slowly, and notice how you feel afterward.

segments.voice: At the end of a checkup a doctor might say: you're healthy. It's good news, and it's mostly a list of things that aren't there. No fever. Nothing broken. Numbers in range. The classical Ayurveda texts have a definition of a healthy person too. It starts in the body, the way a checkup does, then keeps going, and ends with a word Krishna uses on a battlefield. It's also the end of the week, so after the definition, a look back.
screen: `YOU'RE HEALTHY.` → `A LIST OF WHAT ISN'T THERE.` → `A DEFINITION THAT KEEPS GOING.`

segments.voice: The Sushruta Samhita, one of Ayurveda's classics, defines a healthy person in one verse. In paraphrase: the one whose doshas are in balance, whose digestive fire is balanced, whose tissues and wastes do their work, and whose self, senses and mind are prasanna, clear and content, is called svastha, healthy. Body first. Then it keeps going, inward. That last word has a famous echo in the Bhagavad Gita. On the battlefield, Arjuna asks Krishna: what is a person of steady wisdom like? How do they speak, sit, walk? Krishna's answer winds through craving and anger, and then, in paraphrase: one who moves among the things of the world with the senses in hand, free of grabbing and pushing away, comes to prasada, clearness. In that clearness every sorrow ends, and for the one whose mind is clear, understanding soon stands steady. So here's the teaching, in Hindu terms: being well isn't only a body without a fever. It reaches the self. A clear, settled mind is part of health, and part of the path, and Hindus seek it in daily prayer, in japa, in the quiet after a puja. This path holds Sushruta's verse as a lens, not a checklist, and a real checkup still belongs with a doctor. And that's the week: blessed hands, chanting for the sick, plants called mothers, the waters, Dhanvantari, food for a clear mind, and the word for well.
screen: `SVASTHA: BODY, THEN MIND.` · `THE GITA'S ECHO: STEADY WISDOM.` · `IN CLEARNESS, EVERY SORROW ENDS.` · `HEALTH REACHES THE SELF.`

segments.voice: Start with the senses: what can you hear right now, and what can you see, even with your eyes half closed? Then the mind, busy or settled, with no grading, just a look. Last, the simplest question: is there any clearness here at all, even a little? If you pray, rest there with a name of God. If you don't, simply rest with whatever is there.
